passage_changes.passage: Pakistan and Afghanistan have shared a difficult relationship for decades, shaped by changes of government inside Afghanistan and by the border between the two countries. Afghanistan's monarchy ended in 1973 and was followed by a nationalist regime, then communist rule backed by the Soviet Union. Pakistan supported Afghan Mujahideen factions during the period of Soviet military intervention, and later became one of the few countries to recognise the Taliban regime. After the Taliban regained full control in 2021, Pakistan initially welcomed the development, expecting strategic alignment. Tensions soon resurfaced, however, as cross-border militancy continued. Pakistan alleges that the Afghan Taliban is sheltering the TTP, while Afghan governments have historically disputed the legitimacy of the Durand Line, which Pakistan treats as a permanent international border. Afghanistan argues that the agreement behind the line was signed under colonial pressure, while Pakistan says it inherited the boundary after independence in 1947. Clashes at disputed checkpoints escalated into direct military confrontation, and the fighting drew a sharp response from India, which condemned Pakistan's attacks. Pakistan's traditional doctrine of strategic depth has also been eroded, since the Taliban has reached out to India and reduced Pakistan's leverage over Kabul. The result is a conflict in which border disputes, militancy and trade disruption reinforce one another.

In March 2026, the Supreme Court of India ruled that parental income alone cannot be the sole criterion for determining the creamy layer status of Other Backward Classes (OBCs). The judgement responds to a concern about consistency in how the creamy layer is determined. The Court pointed to an uneven system in which children of government employees are assessed on the basis of parental rank or post, while children of employees in public sector undertakings and the private sector are assessed mainly on parental income. It described this unequal method as inconsistent and in conflict with the principle of equality.

Commentary on the ruling holds that rank or position in employment reflects social status and influence better than income alone. Commentary on the ruling also notes that long years of service may raise salary levels without necessarily improving social standing, especially for lower-level employees. A post-based criterion applied across all sectors could, in this commentary's view, provide a fair and consistent way to identify the creamy layer.

The ruling has drawn criticism. Private-sector employers have no standardised rank hierarchy, which makes post-based classification difficult. Critics also argue that income strongly shapes access to quality education and opportunities, and that high-income families in the private sector could keep reservation benefits, limiting opportunities for economically weaker OBC groups.

Measuring an economy requires a fixed reference period against which later figures are compared. This reference, known as the base year, is used to calculate price-adjusted output, so that changes in the size of an economy are not confused with changes in prices. As economies evolve, a base year that once reflected the production structure gradually becomes outdated. New industries grow, consumer habits shift, and the relative importance of sectors changes. Statisticians therefore revise the base year at intervals, rebuilding national accounts on a newer structure. Each revision also gives an opportunity to improve methods and draw on fresh information. Administrative records, periodic household surveys and financial data can capture activities that older estimates may have missed, such as small unregistered enterprises and digital services. The methods used to remove price effects from output figures can also be refined, which sharpens the estimate of value added in key sectors. International guidelines for national accounts are updated periodically, and revisions help countries keep their figures comparable with global standards. Because gross domestic product guides budget planning, investment decisions and assessments of fiscal health, a revision can change reported growth rates and ratios even when the real economy has not changed. For this reason, official releases usually set out the revised base year and the improved estimation methods, so that analysts can interpret trends correctly.

World Tuberculosis Day is observed every year to raise awareness about a disease that is spread through the air and is both preventable and curable. The day also seeks to accelerate global efforts to eliminate the disease, and this year's message stresses that countries lead the response while people power it. The disease has been known to science for more than a century, yet it continues to affect people around the world. Public health bodies monitor the disease through a few core measures. Incidence is measured as a rate per 100,000 people. Deaths are tracked as a separate measure. Comparing these measures against a base year allows analysts to judge whether the response is working. The latest global report reviews the situation for recent years. It looks at how the caseload is spread across countries and regions, and it identifies where most of the burden sits. Such findings help governments and international partners decide where to direct diagnostic tools, treatment programmes and financial support. Concentration matters because a small group of countries often carries most of the caseload. Targeted action in those places therefore matters a great deal for global totals. Officials regularly compare countries, track trends and review progress, so that resources reach the places where they are needed most.

The Academy Awards, popularly known as the Oscars, are among the best-known honours in the film industry. The 98th edition of the awards was held in Los Angeles to celebrate excellence in global cinema. The awards recognise artistic and technical achievements, and they cover a wide range of work, including acting, directing and writing. They are presented by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, an organisation based in the United States. The annual ceremony takes place at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles. Over the years the awards have grown in scope, and the categories have expanded from 12 to 24. Students of current affairs are expected to know the year of the ceremony, the city where it is held and the body that presents the awards, since these basic details are often used in questions. Because the awards cover technical as well as artistic work, they recognise many of the people who contribute to a film. Keeping these basic details in mind helps a candidate answer questions on the Oscars with confidence.

Several international bodies were in the news in March 2026, and their work shows how countries cooperate across borders. Argentina has decided to leave the World Health Organization, a specialised agency of the United Nations, after giving the required notice period. The move was linked to concerns about sovereignty and dissatisfaction with the organisation's response to COVID-19. The WHO remains responsible for global public health governance, and India falls under its South-East Asia Regional Office. India also has a role in gender equality forums. Its Women and Child Development Minister is to represent the country at the 70th Session of the Commission on the Status of Women in New York, and India has been re-elected to the Commission. The Commission is the principal intergovernmental body of the United Nations dedicated to gender equality and women's empowerment. In the Bay of Bengal region, India hosted a youth programme under BIMSTEC, a grouping that aims to promote cooperation in trade, connectivity, energy and sustainable development. The programme was organised by the Ministry of External Affairs and Bharat Scouts, and it aimed to boost youth engagement and regional cooperation. In Europe, India and Croatia discussed trade and investment opportunities during talks with the Special Envoy for the Three Seas Initiative, a regional platform of European Union countries located between three major seas. Together, these developments show how governments use global and regional forums to pursue shared goals.

India's relationship with Afghanistan rests on historical, cultural and developmental foundations. Gandhara, a region that is part of modern-day Afghanistan, was one of the Mahajanapadas of the Vedic Age, and the Bamiyan Buddhas reflect the influence of Buddhism in the country. Afghanistan is also strategically important, because it acts as a crossroad between South Asia and Central Asia as well as between South Asia and the Middle East. Over the years, India has backed projects that support Afghanistan's energy, agriculture and drinking water needs, as well as its democratic institutions. Dams, roads and public buildings are among the projects India has built or helped build. One gas pipeline would carry natural gas from Turkmenistan through Afghanistan and Pakistan to India, while another highway gives Afghanistan a route to a port in Iran that bypasses Pakistan. India has also engaged the Taliban regime at a senior diplomatic level. Afghanistan's position on the border differs, since it does not officially recognise the Durand Line. Repeated closures of the Torkham crossing have also hurt Afghan trade and pushed Kabul toward Iranian routes, which shows how trade and border policy are linked. Taken together, India's engagement covers history, development and trade.

Relations between India and Canada came under strain after a series of disputes. Diplomatic ties between the two countries had been in place since 1947, so the strain was felt in a long-established relationship. Canada's Prime Minister alleged a possible link between Indian agents and the killing of a Sikh separatist leader, Hardeep Singh Nijjar. The disagreement deepened when both countries expelled diplomats and froze consular services, which made it harder for citizens to access official help. Routine services for citizens became harder to obtain for a time. India viewed Canada's tolerance of separatist groups as a threat to its territorial integrity, and this added to the mistrust between the two governments. The rifts also reached the economy. Trade negotiations were halted, bilateral trade slowed and uncertainty was created for Canadian investments in India. Business planning became harder because of the uncertainty around trade ties and new investment in the region. Students and job applicants felt the impact as visa processing for Indians became slower. The standoff was also seen as a risk to India's standing in major global forums and to its ties with some of Canada's closest partners. Taken together, these developments show how a single dispute can spread into trade, visas and wider diplomacy.

After independence, the government recognised that some communities beyond the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes remained socially and educationally backward. A later Backward Classes Commission was set up under a constitutional provision that allows the state to investigate the conditions of such classes and suggest measures for their advancement. Its work involved studying the social standing of these communities across the country before recommending remedies.

The Commission's central recommendation concerned reservation in government jobs for backward communities. The government of the time later implemented this recommendation, and the decision reserved 27% of government jobs for these groups.

In a later judgement, the Supreme Court examined the validity of the reservation. It upheld the scheme with conditions. These included a limit on the total reserved share, a bar on reservation in promotions, and a requirement that advanced members of the class be excluded. The Court also held that the carry-forward rule for backlog vacancies could remain valid, and it called for a permanent statutory body to handle complaints about inclusion in the list.

The legal status of gender and sexual minorities in India has changed through a sequence of court judgments, a statute and government initiatives. LGBTQ+ is a broad category covering people who identify in different ways, and the terminology used varies with historical, cultural and social contexts. Discrimination can be based on sexual orientation, gender expression, gender identity or sex characteristics. Over the years the Supreme Court has been asked to decide several questions about these rights, including the status of relations between consenting adults and whether marriage between people of the same sex can be legally recognised. Parliament has also enacted a law meant to protect the rights of transgender persons and provide for their welfare. Alongside legal change, the government has launched support programmes that offer rehabilitation, identity documents, shelter and skill training. Countries across the world have taken different paths on these questions, and their rights records are compared through indices. Understanding the sequence of cases, statutes and schemes helps place the current debate on the Amendment Bill in context. Such schemes are designed to support people who face social exclusion, and the benefits they offer are meant to reach communities that have historically been marginalised. A useful way to study this topic is to connect each legal development with the rights it recognised and the practical support that followed it.

Official statistics are only as good as the information fed into them. Modern statistical systems combine several sources to improve coverage of the informal sector. Tax collections on goods and services offer a timely view of business activity, while registrations of motor vehicles reflect demand and mobility. Financial management systems record government spending and receipts, which helps in measuring public sector activity. Labour surveys provide information on employment, including work that does not follow a conventional pattern. Such sources help capture household enterprises and digital activity that are hard to observe directly. Measurement also depends on how prices are handled. When output is converted into real terms, a careful price adjustment gives a more accurate picture of value added across the economy. Statisticians must also decide who is counted within the economy, and newer estimates aim to include workers who earn income in unconventional ways. Better coverage does not change the underlying economy, but it reduces the risk that real activity goes unrecorded. Users of these statistics should therefore read revised figures alongside the notes that explain changes in methodology.

India is one of the world's major buyers of defence equipment, and its purchases shape both its military capability and its relationships with foreign suppliers. In the most recent SIPRI assessment, covering 2021 to 2025, India kept a high position among the world's arms importers. However, its total arms imports during this period were lower than in the earlier phase, a change linked to a growing push for domestic production. Over the past several years, the government has focused on building a stronger defence manufacturing base at home. Procurement policy was revised to prioritise Indian-made products over foreign purchases, which signals a clear preference for local industry. To support this shift, industrial corridors have been created in certain states to bring together manufacturers and suppliers. Foreign investment is also allowed in the defence sector through both automatic and government routes, while a dedicated initiative supports start-ups and small firms working on innovation. Taken together, these steps aim to reduce dependence on imported weapons and to turn India into a larger producer and exporter of defence equipment. The way procurement rules are designed determines how much equipment is sourced from abroad and how much is built locally. Industry players are being encouraged to take on more of the manufacturing work, which supports the aim of building a broader defence industrial base.

India has built a layered response to tuberculosis that combines national planning, direct support for patients and digital tools for monitoring. The national strategy is a roadmap to eliminate the disease, and its timeline is set to finish ahead of the global schedule. Its goals include steep reductions in incidence and in deaths, measured against the baseline set for the plan. Patients receive support as well as treatment. Under a direct benefit transfer scheme, every person registered for treatment receives a monthly amount meant for nutrition. Citizens and organisations can also take part. Individuals, non-governmental organisations and corporates are encouraged to support patients through a community-driven model. Diagnosis has also improved. A molecular test based on the polymerase chain reaction principle is now part of the toolkit, helping health workers detect the disease. Urban areas receive focused attention because they can contain hotspots where transmission is concentrated. Local interventions are designed to respond to such pockets rather than treating the whole city uniformly. Such local work is carried out under the separately launched TB Mukt Urban Ward Initiative. Progress is visible in the national figures, which show that the disease rate has fallen in recent years. Officials use digital platforms to monitor the programme, raise public awareness and invite citizen participation.

India honours its writers through several prestigious literary awards. Among these, the Jnanpith Award is regarded as one of the country's oldest and highest literary honours, and it is often compared to a Nobel Prize for Indian literature. The award is given only to Indian authors for outstanding contributions to literature, and it recognises lifetime work rather than a single book. It is not awarded posthumously. The works considered can be in any of the languages listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, as well as English. The award is presented by Bharatiya Jnanpith. Another major honour is the Sahitya Akademi Award, which recognises outstanding literary works and is given to Indian citizens across many languages. The Sahitya Akademi announced its 2025 awards to 24 authors for literary excellence in different languages and genres, from novels to memoirs. Together, these awards highlight the range of literature produced in India and give writers national recognition for their contribution to Indian letters. The Jnanpith is awarded for a writer's overall body of work rather than one book or one year of writing, so each recognition reflects sustained literary effort. Awards of this kind also help readers discover writing in many languages, from the languages of the Eighth Schedule to English, and they show how literature in India is shared across regions and communities.

facts.title: Background of Bilateral Ties
facts.summary: India and Canada established diplomatic ties in 1947 and cooperate in trade, nuclear energy and space. Bilateral trade was worth USD 30.9 billion in 2024. Their nuclear links include the CIRUS reactor (1954) and the Nuclear Cooperation Agreement (2013), and ISRO and the Canadian Space Agency collaborate in space.
facts: Bilateral trade worth USD 30.9 billion in 2024.
Nuclear Cooperation Agreement (2013) facilitates uranium supply and oversight.
Canada assisted India in building a nuclear research reactor named CIRUS in 1954.
Space collaboration between ISRO and the Canadian Space Agency.
Joint research collaboration exists between the two countries.
